title: Human Flourishing, Heidegger's Revealing, Hickel & Aristotle's Good Life
subject: Science, Technology, and Society
description: Martin Heidegger's 'The Question Concerning Technology' (poiesis, aletheia, enframing, standing-reserve, art), Jason Hickel's de-development paradigm, and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics (eudaimonia & virtue).
sourceFile: STS-WK1-MTWThF A book reference in STS.pdf, STS MIDTERM REVIEWER.docx

questions.question: What are the two common definitions of technology that Martin Heidegger calls 'instrumental' and 'anthropological'?
options: Technology as a divine miracle and as an artistic hobby
Technology as a means to an end (instrumental) and as a human activity (anthropological)
Technology as pure mathematics and as biological evolution
Technology as profit and as entertainment
questions.answer: Technology as a means to an end (instrumental) and as a human activity (anthropological)
questions.explanation: Heidegger notes both definitions are 'correct'—technology is an instrumentum and human activity—but do not yet reveal its deeper truth/essence.

questions.question: What does Martin Heidegger mean by his famous statement, 'The essence of technology is by no means anything technological'?
options: Machines do not exist in physical reality
Technology's true essence lies not in gears, gadgets, or functions, but in how it serves as a mode of revealing truth and shaping our way of seeing reality
Only ancient wooden tools count as technology
Technology should be completely banned by governments
questions.answer: Technology's true essence lies not in gears, gadgets, or functions, but in how it serves as a mode of revealing truth and shaping our way of seeing reality
questions.explanation: Regarding technology merely as 'neutral' tools makes us blind to its essence as a mode of revealing.

questions.question: Match Heidegger's three foundational Greek terms—aletheia, poiesis, and techne—to their meanings:
options: aletheia: unhiddenness/truth/disclosure; poiesis: bringing-forth/producing (also poetry); techne: skill, art, or craft
aletheia: mining coal; poiesis: industrial factory; techne: banking system
aletheia: happiness; poiesis: citizenship; techne: political election
aletheia: planetary orbit; poiesis: natural selection; techne: psychoanalysis
questions.answer: aletheia: unhiddenness/truth/disclosure; poiesis: bringing-forth/producing (also poetry); techne: skill, art, or craft
questions.explanation: In Heidegger's analysis, ancient techne belonged to poiesis—a harmonious bringing-forth that reveals truth (aletheia).

questions.question: Using Heidegger's silver chalice example, which pairing correctly identifies Aristotle's four causes?
options: Material: silver; Formal: chalice shape; Final: sacrificial rite (purpose); Efficient: silversmith (artisan)
Material: silversmith; Formal: silver; Final: table; Efficient: fire
Material: water; Formal: gold; Final: museum sale; Efficient: customer
Material: clay; Formal: square; Final: sacrifice; Efficient: sunlight
questions.answer: Material: silver; Formal: chalice shape; Final: sacrificial rite (purpose); Efficient: silversmith (artisan)
questions.explanation: Heidegger traces causality back to the Greek 'aition' (being responsible or indebted to), revealing a poetic bringing-forth.

questions.question: How did the ancient Greek understanding of 'cause' (aition) differ from the modern mechanical notion of cause and effect?
options: Aition meant random coincidence without responsibility
Aition meant indebtedness and being responsible for bringing something forth (e.g., Greeks revered the sun out of indebtedness, not merely as a mechanical energy source)
Aition meant forcing nature to obey factory schedules
Aition applied only to legal court trials
questions.answer: Aition meant indebtedness and being responsible for bringing something forth (e.g., Greeks revered the sun out of indebtedness, not merely as a mechanical energy source)
questions.explanation: Tracing instrumentality back to fourfold aition uncovers the cooperative, poetic character of bringing-forth.

questions.question: How does modern technology's mode of revealing differ from ancient techne/poiesis?
options: Modern technology patiently waits for seasons without disturbing nature
Modern technology is an aggressive 'challenging-forth' (Herausfordern) that sets upon nature and forces it to yield energy and resources on demand
Modern technology never touches natural resources
Modern technology is identical to medieval poetry
questions.answer: Modern technology is an aggressive 'challenging-forth' (Herausfordern) that sets upon nature and forces it to yield energy and resources on demand
questions.explanation: Contrast a wooden bridge built over the Rhine (working with the river) with a hydroelectric dam blocking and challenging the Rhine to yield power.

questions.question: In Heidegger's philosophy, what is 'Enframing' (Gestell)?
options: Hanging oil paintings inside wooden picture frames
The pervasive modern mindset that puts nature 'in a box' as a calculable, orderable, controllable system of resources
A photographic rule of nine equal squares
Refusing to own any smartphone or computer
questions.answer: The pervasive modern mindset that puts nature 'in a box' as a calculable, orderable, controllable system of resources
questions.explanation: Enframing blocks poiesis by treating all of reality—and even people—solely as raw data or material to be controlled.

questions.question: What does Heidegger call everything—including nature and humans—when Enframing reduces it to mere inventory waiting on call to be extracted, stockpiled, and consumed?
options: Eudaimonia
Standing-reserve (Bestand)
Catharsis
Aletheia
questions.answer: Standing-reserve (Bestand)
questions.explanation: Under Enframing, the Earth becomes a giant gas station and people become 'human resources'—mere standing-reserve.

questions.question: Why did Heidegger write 'Questioning is the piety of thought,' and what did 'piety' mean to him here?
options: Piety meant blind obedience to television commercials
Piety meant obedience and submission to what reflective thinking elicits, leading us to wonder at our true place in the universe
Piety meant performing religious rituals before turning on a computer
Piety meant memorizing engineering formulas without asking why
questions.answer: Piety meant obedience and submission to what reflective thinking elicits, leading us to wonder at our true place in the universe
questions.explanation: Stepping back to question technology opens us to deeper truths beyond mere utility.

questions.question: How did Heidegger contrast 'calculative thinking' and 'meditative thinking'?
options: Calculative thinking orders and controls nature into systems for utility; meditative thinking lets nature reveal itself without forcing it
Calculative thinking is only for poets; meditative thinking is only for accountants
Calculative thinking is evil and should be surgically removed; meditative thinking solves math equations
They are exact synonyms in German
questions.answer: Calculative thinking orders and controls nature into systems for utility; meditative thinking lets nature reveal itself without forcing it
questions.explanation: Humans possess both faculties, yet fear of unpredictability pushes modern society toward calculative dominance.

questions.question: What is the ultimate 'danger' of Enframing according to Heidegger, and why does merely refusing technology fail to free us?
options: The danger is battery failure; refusing technology solves everything instantly
The danger is losing our essence and becoming standing-reserve ourselves; whether we blindly affirm or deny technology, or treat it as 'neutral,' we remain unfree and chained to it
The danger is too much poetry in schools
The danger is running out of silver chalices
questions.answer: The danger is losing our essence and becoming standing-reserve ourselves; whether we blindly affirm or deny technology, or treat it as 'neutral,' we remain unfree and chained to it
questions.explanation: Heidegger warned we are delivered over to technology in the worst way when we regard it as something purely neutral.

questions.question: Quoting poet Friedrich Hölderlin ('But where danger is, grows the saving power also'), what does Heidegger propose as a 'way out of Enframing'?
options: Building larger coal mines
Art (poiesis / techne), which awakens meditative thinking and reveals nature as poetic rather than mere standing-reserve
Replacing all humans with AI
Accelerating fossil fuel stockpiling
questions.answer: Art (poiesis / techne), which awakens meditative thinking and reveals nature as poetic rather than mere standing-reserve
questions.explanation: Art restores a poetic dwelling upon the Earth ('...poetically man dwells upon this Earth') and balances calculative control.

questions.question: In Jason Hickel's article 'Forget developing poor countries, it's time to de-develop rich countries,' what is his central critique of the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)?
options: Their goal of eradicating poverty is bad
Beneath the fanfare, their main strategy for ending poverty is still conventional economic growth—a 70-year strategy that hasn't worked and worsens ecological overshoot
They rely too heavily on Cuba and Costa Rica
They require rich nations to reduce advertising
questions.answer: Beneath the fanfare, their main strategy for ending poverty is still conventional economic growth—a 70-year strategy that hasn't worked and worsens ecological overshoot
questions.explanation: Hickel notes that since 1980 the global economy grew 380%, yet people living under $5/day increased by over 1.1 billion.

questions.question: By how much is average global consumption currently overshooting Earth's annual biocapacity, and what is the sustainable per-person threshold?
options: Overshooting by 5%; sustainable threshold is 10 global hectares
Overshooting by more than 50% each year; sustainable threshold is roughly 1.8 global hectares per person annually
Under-consuming by 50%; threshold is 0.1 hectares
Overshooting by 200%; threshold is 50 hectares
questions.answer: Overshooting by more than 50% each year; sustainable threshold is roughly 1.8 global hectares per person annually
questions.explanation: Global hectares measure resource use and waste; US/Canada consume ~8 ha per person and Europe ~4.7 ha, far above 1.8 ha.

questions.question: Which economist did Hickel cite who proposed getting rich countries to 'catch down' to appropriate levels of consumption instead of pushing poor countries to 'catch up'?
options: Peter Edward
Immanuel Kant
Isaac Newton
Bill Joy
questions.answer: Peter Edward
questions.explanation: Peter Edward argued we should look at societies achieving long, happy lives at sustainable consumption levels as exemplars of efficient living.

questions.question: Which country did Hickel highlight as achieving life expectancy comparable to the US (~79 years) and top literacy rates with a GDP per capita of only $6,000 and 1.9 global hectares?
options: Canada
Cuba (alongside high-happiness Costa Rica at 1/4 US income)
Germany
Singapore
questions.answer: Cuba (alongside high-happiness Costa Rica at 1/4 US income)
questions.explanation: Cuba and Costa Rica demonstrate high life expectancy, literacy, and happiness without excessive ecological footprints.

questions.question: Why does Hickel say terms like 'de-growth' or 'de-development' face pushback, and what positive alternative framing/policies does he cite?
options: They sound repulsive to ideas of human progress; instead he cites Latin America's indigenous 'buen vivir' (good living) and the Skidelskys' proposals (banning advertising, shorter work week, basic income)
Because nobody cares about climate change; he proposes tripling fossil fuel use
Because 70% of rich-country citizens want more consumption; he proposes abolishing weekends
Because GDP measures happiness perfectly
questions.answer: They sound repulsive to ideas of human progress; instead he cites Latin America's indigenous 'buen vivir' (good living) and the Skidelskys' proposals (banning advertising, shorter work week, basic income)
questions.explanation: 70% in middle/high-income nations already believe overconsumption puts society at risk; we must slow down voluntarily or climate change will force us.

questions.question: According to Aristotle in 'Nicomachean Ethics,' what is 'the good'?
options: Accumulating maximum luxury gadgets
That at which all human activities, arts, inquiries, and pursuits aim
Avoiding all community interaction
Maximizing short-term sensory pleasure regardless of harm
questions.answer: That at which all human activities, arts, inquiries, and pursuits aim
questions.explanation: Aristotle opens Nicomachean Ethics by observing that every human action aims at some good.

questions.question: What are the Greek roots of 'eudaimonia,' and how is the concept defined in Chapter 6?
options: eu ('good') + daimon ('spirit') — human flourishing marked by living well, doing well, happiness, and excellence
eu ('rich') + demos ('crowd') — winning political elections
ek ('out') + techne ('tool') — building industrial machines
auto ('self') + nomos ('law') — living alone in a bubble
questions.answer: eu ('good') + daimon ('spirit') — human flourishing marked by living well, doing well, happiness, and excellence
questions.explanation: Eudaimonia is a flourishing life of meaningful endeavors that empower a person to become their best version.

questions.question: Why does Aristotle identify happiness (eudaimonia) as the ultimate end of human action?
options: Because we always choose happiness for its own sake and never merely as a means to something else
Because honor, wealth, and power require no effort
Because happiness only lasts for five minutes
Because virtue prevents happiness
questions.answer: Because we always choose happiness for its own sake and never merely as a means to something else
questions.explanation: Things like wealth, honor, and pleasure are pursued for the sake of happiness, whereas happiness is chosen solely for itself.

questions.question: How does Aristotle's view of happiness differ from Hedonism?
options: Hedonism defines happiness as maximizing sensate pleasure and avoiding pain; Aristotle defines it as living a life of virtue and excellence
Hedonism values discipline; Aristotle values junk food
They are completely identical philosophies
Hedonism comes from Nicomachean Ethics
questions.answer: Hedonism defines happiness as maximizing sensate pleasure and avoiding pain; Aristotle defines it as living a life of virtue and excellence
questions.explanation: Sensate convenience (like eating sugary processed food or neglecting the environment) undermines true flourishing.

questions.question: In the Midterm Reviewer's comparison table of happiness perspectives, which perspective links happiness to a hormonal reward system (dopamine/oxytocin) promoting survival?
options: Neurology
Hedonism
Eudaimonia
Behaviorism
questions.answer: Neurology
questions.explanation: Psychology views emotional well-being; Behaviorism views positive-action emotions; Neurology views dopamine/oxytocin; Hedonism views pleasure; Eudaimonia views virtue/growth.

questions.question: What are Aristotle's two kinds of virtue, and how is each acquired?
options: Intellectual virtue (owes birth and growth to teaching, requiring experience and time) and Moral virtue (comes about as a result of habit)
Physical virtue (born innate) and Financial virtue (inherited)
Technological virtue and Commercial virtue
Calculative virtue and Passive virtue
questions.answer: Intellectual virtue (owes birth and growth to teaching, requiring experience and time) and Moral virtue (comes about as a result of habit)
questions.explanation: Excellence of character is NOT innate without practice—it is cultivated through constant, disciplined habit.

questions.question: True or False according to Chapter 6: 'The good life means I make sure I improve myself without needing to consider others.'
options: True—Aristotle taught pure self-centered isolation.
False—the good life does not happen in a bubble; virtuous actions affect both the individual self and the greater community.
True—only one person can flourish at a time.
False—only animals can flourish.
questions.answer: False—the good life does not happen in a bubble; virtuous actions affect both the individual self and the greater community.
questions.explanation: Aristotelian flourishing requires shared well-being—others must flourish alongside us.

questions.question: How do science and technology relate to Aristotle's concept of the good life?
options: Science and technology are inherently evil and never aid human flourishing
They are among the highest expressions of human faculties that help us thrive, provided we ground ourselves in virtue to avoid corruption
They automatically guarantee moral virtue without human discipline
They replace the need for ethical standards
questions.answer: They are among the highest expressions of human faculties that help us thrive, provided we ground ourselves in virtue to avoid corruption
questions.explanation: Virtue guides how we use powerful scientific and technological capabilities responsibly.

questions.question: What parallel exists between Heidegger's 'Enframing' and Hickel's critique of growth-obsessed development?
options: Both celebrate turning the entire planet into a limitless industrial warehouse
Both warn against reducing Earth and human flourishing to quantifiable extraction/consumption, urging a shift toward qualitative harmony and sufficiency
Both argue poor nations should triple their carbon footprint
Both reject art and community well-being
questions.answer: Both warn against reducing Earth and human flourishing to quantifiable extraction/consumption, urging a shift toward qualitative harmony and sufficiency
questions.explanation: We have been 'enframed' by the notion of endless growth, forgetting qualitative well-being and planetary boundaries.

questions.question: Why does Heidegger compare a traditional watermill to a modern hydroelectric power plant on the Rhine River?
options: To show the watermill moves in harmony with the river's natural rhythm, whereas the hydroplant dams and forces the river into standing-reserve
To prove watermills generate more megawatts than hydroplants
To argue rivers do not exist in Germany
To praise calculative stockpiling over poiesis
questions.answer: To show the watermill moves in harmony with the river's natural rhythm, whereas the hydroplant dams and forces the river into standing-reserve
questions.explanation: The hydroelectric plant exemplifies modern challenging-forth—unlocking, transforming, storing, and distributing energy on demand.

questions.question: When is the human person 'swallowed by technology' according to Chapter 4?
options: Whenever someone uses a pencil to write
When we stay constantly plugged online, lose authentic personal encounters, and refuse to surrender polluting conveniences that harm the Earth
Whenever we admire fine art in a museum
When we practice meditative thinking in nature
questions.answer: When we stay constantly plugged online, lose authentic personal encounters, and refuse to surrender polluting conveniences that harm the Earth
questions.explanation: Recognizing human limits protects our essence from being consumed by technological conveniences.

questions.question: In the Midterm Reviewer, which four ancient Greek components were linked to human flourishing?
options: Phronesis (practical wisdom), Friendship, Wealth, and Power
Digital phones, Global travel, AI, and Fast food
Cuneiform, Papyrus, Gunpowder, and Steam
Enframing, Standing-reserve, Mining, and Coal
questions.answer: Phronesis (practical wisdom), Friendship, Wealth, and Power
questions.explanation: Classical flourishing valued practical wisdom and friendship alongside sufficient external goods, whereas modern conceptions emphasize comfort and global networking.

questions.question: What did recent consumer research cited by Hickel show about people in middle- and high-income countries?
options: 100% want to double their plastic waste
70% believe overconsumption is putting the planet and society at risk and that we should buy and own less without losing happiness
Only 2% have heard of climate change
Most believe Earth has infinite resources
questions.answer: 70% believe overconsumption is putting the planet and society at risk and that we should buy and own less without losing happiness
questions.explanation: Public intuition already senses that endless accumulation does not produce happiness.

questions.question: How did Heidegger view the relationship between 'what is correct' and 'what is true'?
options: They are complete opposites with no bridge
What is correct (e.g., instrumental utility) is not yet the full truth, but understanding what is correct can lead us toward discovering what is true
Only machines can determine truth
Truth is irrelevant to philosophy
questions.answer: What is correct (e.g., instrumental utility) is not yet the full truth, but understanding what is correct can lead us toward discovering what is true
questions.explanation: Recognizing technology's instrumental correctness is a stepping stone to pondering its deeper essence as revealing.

questions.question: In Chapter 6's Reading Exercise, which statements are FALSE regarding Aristotle's Good Life?
options: 'One does not need to eat healthfully to live the good life' and 'Excellence of character is innate and does not have to be practiced'
'Eudaimonia means living and doing well' and 'Virtue is the constant practice of the good'
'Happiness is the ultimate end' and 'Aristotle wrote Nicomachean Ethics'
'Intellectual and moral are two kinds of virtue'
questions.answer: 'One does not need to eat healthfully to live the good life' and 'Excellence of character is innate and does not have to be practiced'
questions.explanation: Healthy living and disciplined habit are central to practicing virtue and attaining flourishing.

questions.question: In Chapter 5's 'The Magician's Twin' reflection activity, what is 'scientism'?
options: Using scientific data within ethical limits
Treating empirical science as the sole source of all truth and meaning, or elevating science to an unquestioned quasi-religious authority
Studying marine biology in college
Recycling household waste
questions.answer: Treating empirical science as the sole source of all truth and meaning, or elevating science to an unquestioned quasi-religious authority
questions.explanation: C.S. Lewis warned that unchecked scientism—like magic—can seek power over nature and humanity without moral restraint.

questions.question: According to Hickel, if rich nations do not slow down consumption voluntarily, what will force humanity to slow down?
options: Lack of advertising agencies
Climate change, collapsing food systems, and ecological crisis
Too many libraries
Universal basic income
questions.answer: Climate change, collapsing food systems, and ecological crisis
questions.explanation: Rethinking progress is both an ecological imperative and a human development necessity to prevent mass famine and collapse.
